title: Home-Thoughts, from Abroad: date and publication
short: First printed in November 1845 in Dramatic Romances and Lyrics, as part I of a three-part group; DeVane thought it written in England in April 1845.
body: The poem first appeared in Dramatic Romances and Lyrics (1845), number VII of Browning's pamphlet series Bells and Pomegranates. There it was the first of three pieces under the shared title 'Home-Thoughts, from Abroad'; the second ('Here's to Nelson's memory') was later moved elsewhere, and the third became 'Home-Thoughts, from the Sea'. From 1863 Browning reprinted it under the heading 'Dramatic Lyrics', which is why some editions file it there. William DeVane believed Browning wrote it in England in April 1845, recalling his second Italian journey (1844), so the 'abroad' of the title may be imagined rather than actual. The speaker is not necessarily Browning: like most of his lyrics, it is a dramatic utterance.

title: Now that April's there
short: 'There' places the speaker outside England: April is happening in a place he is not.
body: The deictic 'there' (rather than 'here') sets up the whole poem's structure of longing at a distance. Spring is imagined, not seen. The present tense of 'wakes' and 'sees' in the following lines is therefore a present of imagination: the speaker pictures what an Englishman would see on an April morning. April has a long association with the opening of English poetry (Chaucer's General Prologue begins with it), and with the return of birds, a theme the poem develops. Critics have debated whether the exclamatory opening is simple nostalgia or a more anxious, even ironic utterance by an exile.

title: some morning, unaware
short: The new leaves appear without the observer noticing their coming: spring arrives as a surprise.
body: 'Unaware' modifies the person who wakes: he sees, suddenly and without having watched for it, that the trees are in leaf. The word captures the way English spring seems to happen overnight. It also hints at a contrast between the unreflecting native, who takes this for granted, and the exiled speaker, who is all too aware of what he misses. The vague 'whoever' and 'some morning' make the experience general rather than personal.

title: brush-wood sheaf ... elm-tree bole
short: 'Bole' is the trunk of a tree; the 'brush-wood sheaf' is the cluster of small shoots and twigs around its base.
body: 'Bole', a word of Old Norse origin, means the trunk of a tree. English elms often sprouted dense suckers and small twiggy growth around the base of the trunk, which Browning calls a 'sheaf' of brushwood, as if it were bundled like corn. It is these lowest twigs that first come into 'tiny leaf'. The precision of the observation is typical of the poem, which builds its England out of small, exact rural details rather than grand landscape. The elm was a defining tree of the English countryside until Dutch elm disease destroyed most of them in the twentieth century.

title: chaffinch
short: A common English finch whose song is one of the first heard in spring; the first of several native birds the poem names.
body: The chaffinch (Fringilla coelebs) is one of the commonest British birds, a resident whose bright, descending song begins in late winter and becomes general in spring. The poem's England is made largely of birdsong: the chaffinch in stanza one, then the whitethroat, the swallows and the thrush in stanza two. Each is a familiar, unexotic bird, which supports the poem's preference for the modest English scene over the 'gaudy' south at its close.

title: Irregular lines and the exclamation
short: The stanza ends on a short, broken line; the poem's line lengths and rhymes are irregular, mimicking excited speech.
body: The poem does not use a fixed stanza: the first verse paragraph has eight lines, the second twelve, and the line lengths vary from two stresses to five. Rhymes are present but irregularly placed (there / unaware, with 'England' repeated rather than rhymed; sheaf / leaf; bough / now). The dash and the exclamation 'now!' give the effect of breath and impulse, and the repeated 'England' frames the stanza. The form thus enacts spontaneous longing, though, as the thrush lines will suggest, its spontaneity is carefully made.

title: whitethroat; swallows
short: The whitethroat is a small warbler that arrives in England from Africa in late April and builds in hedges; the swallows are also returning migrants.
body: The common whitethroat (Sylvia communis) is a summer visitor to Britain, wintering south of the Sahara and arriving in April, when the male sings and builds courtship nests in hedgerows and brambles. Swallows, too, return from Africa in April and May. Both are migrants: like the speaker, they have been abroad, but unlike him they come home with the season. The poem moves here from April to May, from first leaves to nest-building and blossom.

title: my blossomed pear-tree in the hedge
short: The speaker imagines a specific tree he calls his own, leaning over the field and shedding petals and dew on the clover.
body: With 'my' the poem moves from the general English scene to a remembered personal place: a pear tree growing in a hedgerow, its blossoming branches bending over the meadow. The petals and dewdrops falling 'at the bent spray's edge' are seen with a painter's closeness. The imperative 'Hark' introduces a sound-picture as well, so that sight and hearing combine in the act of memory. Whether the tree is remembered from Browning's own surroundings (his family then lived at New Cross, on the semi-rural edge of London) or belongs only to the speaker is not stated.

title: That's the wise thrush
short: The song thrush characteristically repeats each phrase two or three times; Browning makes the habit a sign of wisdom.
body: Ornithologists have long noted that the song thrush (Turdus philomelos) sings in short phrases, each typically repeated two or more times. Browning turns this natural fact into a witty conceit: the thrush repeats itself so that listeners will not think its first, spontaneous burst a happy accident that it could never repeat. The bird is 'wise' because it knows its art. The lines respond to Romantic celebrations of natural, unpremeditated song, such as Shelley's skylark with its 'unpremeditated art'.

title: The first fine careless rapture
short: Can spontaneous feeling be recaptured? The thrush's repeated song raises the poet's own question about art, memory and repetition.
body: The phrase is the most quoted in the poem. 'Careless' means free from care and unstudied, and 'rapture' is ecstatic joy. The thrush sings twice to show that its rapture can be recovered at will; the speaker, by contrast, can only recapture England through memory. Readers have taken the lines in different ways: as a celebration of natural song; as a comment on the art of the lyric, which repeats and shapes what seems spontaneous; or, in Alison Chapman's reading, as part of the poem's anxiety about whether a lyric voice abroad can ever make its home-thoughts real. The alliteration of f and r gives the phrase its own lilting rapture.

title: hoary dew
short: Dew so heavy it looks white or grey like frost, making the fields look 'rough' in the early morning.
body: 'Hoary', from Old English har (grey, white-haired), describes something whitened as if with age or frost. In the early hours the dew gives the fields a rough, greyish look, but the speaker promises that by noon, when the sun has burnt it off, all will be 'gay', bright and cheerful. 'Noontide' is an old poetic word for midday. The lines move the imagined day forward from dawn to noon, completing the poem's progression from April morning into full May.

title: The buttercups, the little children's dower
short: The buttercups are the treasure or gift of children; 'dower' means an endowment or dowry.
body: A 'dower' is a portion or endowment, originally the property given with a bride or the share a widow received. The buttercups are the children's natural inheritance: golden flowers that cost nothing and that every child may pick, a wealth that belongs to them by right. The metaphor contrasts humble native riches with the showy beauty of the south in the next line. The golden colour of the buttercup also prepares for the comparison with the yellow melon-flower.

title: this gaudy melon-flower
short: The last line returns the speaker to Italy: 'this' melon-flower is in front of him, showy compared with English buttercups.
body: Only at the very end does the poem show where the speaker is: 'this' melon-flower is before his eyes, probably in Italy (the poem itself names no place). 'Gaudy' means showy, garish, over-bright. The comparison of yellows (the large melon blossom and the small buttercup) concludes the poem's preference for the modest English scene over the opulent south. The judgement is plainly partial, and some critics hear irony in it, as of an exile defensively disparaging his surroundings. Victorian Web notes how readings have shifted from simple nostalgia (Symons called it 'a beautiful poem') to Chapman's sense of anxiety and irony.
